analysis.one_liner: Makes it easier to sue and prosecute police officers for misconduct and bans federal chokeholds and no-knock drug warrants.
analysis.headline: The House passed the George Floyd Justice in Policing Act 236-181 on June 25, 2020, but the Senate never voted on it before the Congress ended, leaving police accountability rules unchanged.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it easier to hold police accountable in court. It removes part of the legal shield called qualified immunity that protects officers from lawsuits, lowers the mental-state bar for federally convicting an officer of misconduct, creates a public national registry of police misconduct records, requires departments to report use-of-force data, bans chokeholds and no-knock warrants in drug cases at the federal level, and creates a framework to ban racial profiling. The House passed it in June 2020, but the Senate took no action, and the bill died when that Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.who_benefits: People mistreated by police, their families, and civil rights lawyers gain easier access to federal court, since officers could no longer hide behind qualified immunity and federal prosecutors would only need to show officers acted knowingly or recklessly rather than willfully. Communities of color gain public data on stops, searches, and use of force, a ban on racial profiling, and a public registry that would flag officers with misconduct records before another department hires them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People mistreated by police and civil rights plaintiffs

how_it_helps.text: The bill ends qualified immunity as a defense for local and federal law enforcement officers in civil lawsuits, removing the rule that officers cannot be sued unless the right they violated was already 'clearly established' in prior case law [S4].
It lowers the criminal intent standard for federal prosecutions of officers from 'willful' to 'knowing or reckless,' making federal misconduct convictions easier to obtain [S3].

It creates a public National Police Misconduct Registry of complaints, discipline, termination, and lawsuit records that hiring agencies would have to consult, aimed at stopping officers with records from being rehired elsewhere [S4].

It bans chokeholds and carotid holds and no-knock warrants in drug cases at the federal level and cuts grant money to states that do not ban them, while restricting the use of deadly force to cases where it is necessary [S3].
It gives the Justice Department subpoena power in pattern-or-practice investigations of police departments and lets state attorneys general bring their own such suits [S3].

It requires all law enforcement agencies to report data on stops, searches, use of force, and deaths in custody, broken down by race and ethnicity, with public release and loss of federal grant money for states that do not comply [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Law enforcement officers and their unions bear the biggest cost: officers could be personally sued more easily, and departments face federal oversight, reporting mandates, training requirements, and accreditation rules. State and local governments pay for data systems, body cameras, and compliance, and risk losing federal Byrne and COPS grant money if they do not meet the conditions. Taxpayers fund the authorized spending, which runs to roughly $1 billion in new grant authorizations, and municipalities would pay more in lawsuit settlements and insurance costs.

drawbacks.text: Removing qualified immunity and lowering the intent standard would expose individual officers and their municipalities to substantially more lawsuits and litigation costs, including for split-second decisions made in good faith, which is the central objection from police groups [S4].
The bill ties substantial federal conditions to grant money, effectively pressuring state and local governments to adopt policies through funding threats rather than direct federal law [S4].
The misconduct registry would include even complaints that were investigated and found unfounded, which officers' representatives argue could unfairly brand officers and chill recruitment [S4].

Most policing is regulated by state and local law, so even if enacted, many of the bill's provisions would change practices indirectly through funding conditions and litigation rather than directly, limiting its real-world reach.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real and well-documented gap: federal civil rights prosecutions of officers are rare under the current 'willful' standard, and qualified immunity routinely ends lawsuits against officers before the merits are heard. The costs are real but mainly fall on governments, insurers, and officers themselves through liability, paperwork, and compliance spending. The most serious honest criticism is design: tying so much to grant conditions means enforcement depends on future administrations' willingness to enforce, and the registry's inclusion of unfounded complaints raises fairness concerns for officers. On balance it is a substantial accountability expansion with a real price paid mostly by police institutions.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it on June 25, 2020, and the Senate received it, read it twice, and placed it on its calendar, but no vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

narrative.text: The House Judiciary Committee reported the bill on June 19, 2020, just eleven days after introduction [S6].
The House passed the bill 236-181 on June 25, 2020, with 233 of 233 voting Democrats in favor and only 3 of 197 voting Republicans [S7].
A Republican motion to recommit, which would have replaced the bill's text with a narrower notification measure, failed 180-236, with all 232 voting Democrats opposed [S6].
The Senate received the bill on June 29, 2020, read it twice, and placed it on its legislative calendar on July 20, 2020, where it remained with no vote ever scheduled [S6].
The bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and none of its provisions became law [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Police unions, law enforcement agencies, and officers' insurers are better off because the bill died: qualified immunity remains intact, the national misconduct registry and federal pattern-or-practice subpoena powers were never created, and no federal ban on chokeholds or no-knock drug warrants took effect. Users of the public record gained nothing beyond the House vote itself.

sides.party_line_note: The House vote split almost entirely by party: 233 of 233 voting Democrats voted yes and only 3 of 197 voting Republicans did, and the motion to recommit failed 180-236 along the same lines.

industries.industry: Police unions and law enforcement agencies
industries.note: The bill would strip their main court shield (qualified immunity), lower the bar for federal criminal prosecution, force public disclosure of misconduct records, and condition grant money on bans of chokeholds and no-knock warrants. Its defeat preserved the status quo. This concentrated interest won when the Senate never acted.

Local governments would pay more in lawsuit settlements, insurance premiums, data systems, and compliance costs, though stronger accountability can reduce the most severe misconduct liabilities over time.

The bill routes public grant money through private accreditation bodies, requiring grantees to spend at least 5 percent of awards on gaining accreditation, making these organizations a permanent funded gatekeeper of the reform framework.
Removing qualified immunity and creating new racial-profiling claims with attorney's fees would expand the market for civil rights lawsuits on behalf of victims of police misconduct.
